note: Works for both hello and goodbye among friends. It is really the noun 'cześć' (honour). Note the two digraphs: 'cz' is like English 'ch', 'ść' is a soft 'shch'.

example.en: Hi, how are things with you?

note: Used after dark instead of 'Dzień dobry'. 'Wieczór' is shared across Slavic (Czech 'večer', Russian 'вечер'). Here the adjective comes first, the normal order.
'Do' (until) takes the genitive, so the verbal noun 'zobaczenie' (seeing) ends in '-a'. Slightly less formal than 'Do widzenia', same structure.

en: See you later / Bye for now
note: 'Raz' means 'a time, once'; 'na razie' literally 'for the time being'. Very common casual goodbye, often shortened to 'nara' by young people.

example.en: I have to go, see you!

note: 'Nie ma' (there isn't) is followed by the genitive, hence the structure 'there is nothing to thank for'. The standard reply to 'dziękuję'.
Said when raising a glass and after someone sneezes. 'Zdrowie' (health) is the same root as Russian 'здоровье'; 'na' here takes the accusative.
Literally 'how do you have yourself'. Informal; to a stranger say 'Jak się pan ma?' / 'Jak się pani ma?' with the verb in the third person.
'Słychać' is an impersonal form meaning 'one can hear'. The usual answer is 'Wszystko w porządku' (everything in order) or 'Nic nowego' (nothing new).
'Dobrze' is the adverb from 'dobry' (good); Polish answers 'how are you' with 'well', not 'good'.
'Mi' is the dative of 'ja' (I). The full form is 'Miło mi pana/panią poznać' (pleasant to me to meet you).
First person plural of 'witać' (to greet). Seen on shop doors and town signs ('Witamy w Krakowie'). A single host says 'Witam'.
Polish has no formal 'you' pronoun: you address a stranger in the third person with 'pan' (man) or 'pani' (woman): 'Czy pan mówi po angielsku?' = 'Do you (sir) speak English?'
The formal plural 'you' for a mixed or male group, used with a plural verb. Capitalised 'Państwo' is polite in letters; lower-case 'państwo' also means 'the state'.
Also means 'so, thus', as in 'tak samo' (the same way). Shared with Czech 'tak' and Russian 'так'.
Both 'no' and the verb negator, placed directly before the verb: 'nie wiem' (I don't know). Polish uses double negatives: 'nic nie wiem' (I know nothing).
For sympathy or regret, not for excusing yourself ('Przepraszam'). 'Przykro' is an adverb, 'mi' the dative 'to me', a very common Polish pattern.
The reply to an apology. The double negative is obligatory: 'nic' (nothing) must be paired with 'nie'. 'Szkodzić' means 'to harm', related to 'szkoda' (pity, damage).
Literally 'I am listening'. Used to ask someone to repeat, when a shop assistant turns to you, and as the standard way to answer the phone.
Wishes are in the genitive because an unspoken 'życzę' (I wish) governs that case. The standard birthday greeting.

example.en: All the best on your birthday!

note: Genitive of 'powodzenie' (success), again from the implied 'życzę'. 'Powodzić się' means 'to go well'.
From Latin 'gratulatio'. The '-cja' ending corresponds to English '-tion' in hundreds of loanwords (stacja, informacja).
Poles sing 'Sto lat, sto lat, niech żyje, żyje nam' at birthdays and name days, wishing a hundred years of life. 'Lat' is the genitive plural required after numbers from five up.

en: Come in! / After you! / My treat!
note: First person of 'zapraszać'. Said when opening a door, letting someone go first, or picking up the bill ('Zapraszam' = it's on me).
The normal sign-off in emails and messages, from 'pozdrawiać' (to send greetings). 'Pozdrowienia z Gdańska' = greetings from Gdańsk, on postcards.
'Imię' is a first name; 'nazwisko' is a surname. Answer: 'Mam na imię Tomek' (literally 'I have for name Tomek').

example.target: Jak masz na imię? Mam na imię Kasia.
example.en: What's your name? My name is Kasia.

note: A European loan (Italian 'zero', ultimately Arabic 'ṣifr'). Polish pronounces the 'z' as a clear 'z', never 'ts'.
Agrees like an adjective: 'jeden' (m), 'jedna' (f), 'jedno' (n). Same root as Russian 'один' and Czech 'jeden'.
'Dwa' for masculine and neuter nouns, 'dwie' for feminine ('dwie kawy'), and 'dwaj' or 'dwóch' for groups of men. Nouns after 2, 3 and 4 stay in the nominative plural.
Same Indo-European root as English 'three'. 'Rz' is a digraph pronounced like 'ż' (the 's' in 'measure'), devoiced to 'sh' after 't' here.
Cognate with 'four' and Russian 'четыре'. The ordinal is 'czwarty'.
The nasal 'ę' sounds like 'en' before 'ć'. From five upwards the counted noun goes into the genitive plural: 'pięć złotych', 'pięć minut'.
Cognate with 'six'. Spelled with the soft cluster 'ść'; the 'sz' at the start is a hard 'sh'.
'Si' before a vowel spells the soft 'ś' sound. Compare Czech 'sedm' and Russian 'семь'.
Ordinal 'ósmy' shows the typical o/ó alternation: the ó appears when the following syllable disappears.
Ends in the nasal 'ę' plus 'ć', like 'pięć'. The initial 'dzi' is one soft sound, roughly 'j' in 'jeep'.
Cognate with Latin 'decem' and English 'ten'. The teens and tens are all built on this word.
The teen ending '-naście' comes from 'na dziesięcie' (on ten), so 'jedenaście' is 'one on top of ten'. All teens follow the pattern 'number + -naście'.
'Dwa' + '-naście'. Feminine 'dwie' is not used inside teens: 'dwanaście kobiet'.
Watch the spelling: the 'ć' of 'pięć' drops and the number is written 'piętnaście', not 'pięćnaście'. The same happens in 'dziewiętnaście' (19).
Built on an old dual form of 'dziesięć' (ten). 21 is 'dwadzieścia jeden', simply juxtaposed.
'Trzy' + a plural form of ten. Forty is 'czterdzieści' on the same pattern.
Note the 'cztery' loses its final 'y' when it combines: 'czterdzieści', 'czternaście' (14).
From 50 to 90 the tens use '-dziesiąt', a genitive plural of ten, because 'five' and above govern the genitive, the same rule as 'pięć złotych'.
Cognate with Latin 'centum' and Russian 'сто'. 200 is 'dwieście', 300 'trzysta', 500 'pięćset'.
Spelled with nasal 'ą'. Behaves like a noun: 'dwa tysiące', 'pięć tysięcy'. Compare Russian 'тысяча'.
An adjective, so it agrees: 'pierwszy raz' (first time), 'pierwsza klasa' (first class). Ordinals are also used for dates and hours: 'pierwsza' = one o'clock.

example.target: To mój pierwszy raz w Polsce.
example.en: This is my first time in Poland.

note: Also means 'the other one', as in 'z drugiej strony' (on the other hand). Compare Russian 'другой' (other). 'Drugie danie' is the main course.
Feminine 'trzecia', as in 'trzecia' (three o'clock). The soft 'ci' is the same sound as 'ć'.
Followed by the genitive: 'pół godziny' (half an hour), 'pół litra'. 'Półtora' means one and a half. 'Ó' is pronounced exactly like 'u'.

example.en: Half a kilo of cheese, please.

note: 'Para butów' (a pair of shoes), 'młoda para' (newly-weds). A homonym 'para' also means 'steam'. 'Parę' means 'a few': 'parę minut'.
From 'ród' (clan, lineage), the same root as 'rodzić' (to give birth) and 'rodzice' (parents).
The formal word; in everyday speech people say 'mama'. Historically 'matka' is itself a diminutive of the old word 'mać'.
Compare Russian 'отец'. The vocative 'ojcze' shows the typical c/cz consonant alternation. Everyday word: 'tata'.
A nursery word found in almost every language. Vocative 'mamo!', diminutive 'mamusia'.
Masculine despite the '-a' ending, so adjectives agree in the masculine: 'mój tata'. Vocative 'tato!'.
Cognate with English 'son' through Indo-European. Diminutive 'synek'.
A diminutive in '-ka' of the older 'córa', now the standard word. Compare Czech 'dcera'.
Cognate with 'brother'. The plural 'bracia' is irregular and was originally a collective noun.
Cognate with 'sister'. Genitive plural 'sióstr' shows the o/ó alternation when the ending disappears.

example.en: I have a brother and a sister.

note: A diminutive in '-ek' of 'dziad', which on its own now sounds archaic or rude ('old beggar'). The affectionate form is standard.
Diminutive of 'baba' (old woman), which alone is disrespectful. 'Dzień Babci' (Grandmother's Day) is 21 January.
Spelled with nasal 'ą' and 'ż'. Compare Russian 'муж'. 'Mężczyzna' (man) is derived from it.
The same ancient root as Greek 'gynē' (woman) and Russian 'жена'. 'Żonaty' = married (of a man).
The plural 'dzieci' is irregular. Diminutive 'dzieciak' is casual, like 'kid'.
A strong word, reserved for close friends. For ordinary friends Poles say 'kolega' or 'znajomy' (acquaintance). Feminine 'przyjaciółka'.
From Latin 'collega' via German 'Kollege'. Masculine although it ends in '-a', so it declines like a feminine noun but takes masculine adjectives: 'dobry kolega'.
From 'chłop' (peasant) with the suffix '-ak'. 'Mój chłopak' means 'my boyfriend'; a small boy is 'chłopiec'.
'Moja dziewczyna' = my girlfriend. A little girl is 'dziewczynka' (diminutive '-ka').
Masculine despite the '-a' ending, derived from 'mąż'. Note the cluster 'żcz'. Adjectives agree in the masculine: 'wysoki mężczyzna'.
Of uncertain origin; in the 16th century it was a disparaging term, but it has long been the neutral word. Polite address is 'pani'.
The plural is the unrelated word 'ludzie'. Compare Russian 'человек', Czech 'člověk'.
Plural only, serving as the plural of 'człowiek'. Related to German 'Leute' (people) through Indo-European.
From 'pole' (field): the Polanie were 'the people of the fields'. Nationalities are capitalised in Polish, but 'polski' (Polish, adj.) is not.
Nasal 'ą'. Compare Russian 'сосед'. Plural 'sąsiedzi' with the a/e vowel change typical of masculine personal nouns.
Plural only in everyday use, from the root 'rodzić' (to give birth). 'U rodziców' = at my parents' place.
An early Germanic loan into Slavic (Gothic 'hlaifs', the source of English 'loaf'). 'Ch' is pronounced like 'h'.
Cognate with 'water'. In cafés you will be asked 'gazowana czy niegazowana?' (sparkling or still?).
Compare Russian 'молоко': Polish keeps the short Slavic form without the extra vowel. 'Kawa z mlekiem' = coffee with milk (instrumental).
From 'mazać' (to smear): butter is 'the stuff you spread'. Compare Russian 'масло'.
Poles distinguish 'biały ser' (white curd cheese, twaróg) from 'żółty ser' (yellow cheese, the hard kind).
Formally a diminutive of 'jajo', but it is the everyday word. 'Jajecznica' is scrambled eggs.
Nasal 'ę' before 's'. Compare Russian 'мясо'. 'Bez mięsa' (without meat) is useful for vegetarians.
From 'kura' (hen) via 'kurczę' (chick). On menus 'kurczak' is the meat; the live bird is 'kura'.
Pan-Slavic word (Russian 'рыба'). Carp ('karp') is the traditional Christmas Eve fish in Poland.
From 'ziemia' (earth), like French 'pomme de terre'. Regional synonyms: 'kartofel' (from German) in the south, 'pyra' around Poznań.
Ultimately from Latin 'cepulla' (little onion), which reached Polish through German. The same source gives Italian 'cipolla'.
Cognate with 'apple'. In fast speech the 'ł' is usually silent, so it sounds like 'japko'.
Plural of 'owoc'; Poles normally use the plural as English uses the mass noun 'fruit'.
From 'warzyć' (to boil, to cook): vegetables are 'things you cook'. Singular 'warzywo'.
From German 'Suppe'. Soup opens most Polish dinners; the classics are 'żurek' (sour rye soup), 'barszcz' (beetroot) and 'rosół' (broth).

example.en: There is tomato soup for dinner.

note: Plural; one dumpling is 'pieróg'. 'Pierogi ruskie' are filled with potato and curd cheese and have nothing to do with Russia (the name refers to historic Ruthenia).
From Turkish 'kahve', ultimately Arabic 'qahwa'. 'Kawa po turecku' is unfiltered coffee with grounds in the glass.
Unique in Europe: a blend of Latin 'herba' (herb) and 'thea' (tea), from the old pharmacists' name 'herba thea'. 'Herbata z cytryną' (with lemon) is the Polish default.
From 'pić' (to drink): originally just 'beverage'. 'Duże piwo' is a half-litre.
From Latin 'vinum'. 'Wino czerwone / białe / wytrawne' = red / white / dry wine.
Compare Russian 'сок'. 'Sok pomarańczowy' (orange), 'sok jabłkowy' (apple).
From German 'Zucker'. The '-ie-' drops in other cases: 'bez cukru' (without sugar), 'z cukrem' (with sugar).
Cognate with Latin 'sal' and English 'salt'. The ó becomes o when an ending is added: 'soli' (genitive). The Wieliczka salt mine is 'kopalnia soli'.
Means both dough and a whole cake. The diminutive 'ciastko' is a pastry or cookie, and 'ciasteczka' are both biscuits and browser cookies.
Entered English as 'kielbasa'. The 'ł' is a 'w' sound, so it is 'kyew-BA-sa'. Diminutive 'kiełbaska'.
From French 'restaurant' with the Polish '-cja' ending. Pronounced 'res-tau-RA-tsya', with 'c' as 'ts'.
'Kawa' + the place suffix '-arnia', as in 'piekarnia' (bakery) and 'księgarnia' (bookshop).

example.en: Shall we go to a café?

note: From German 'Kellner'. To call one, say 'Przepraszam!' rather than the noun. Feminine 'kelnerka'.
'Karta' (card) is the menu card; the loanword 'menu' is also used and never changes its ending. 'Karta dań' = list of dishes.
Diminutive of 'stół' (table) with '-ik'. A restaurant table is always 'stolik': 'stolik dla dwóch osób' (table for two).
From 'rachować' (to reckon), a loan from German 'rechnen'. Also means a bank account or a utility bill.
Imperfective; the perfective partner is 'zamówić' ('zamówiłem pizzę' = I ordered a pizza). 'Zamówienie' is an order.
Perfective future of 'prosić'. The polite way to order or buy anything, followed by the accusative: 'Poproszę kawę', 'Poproszę bilet'.
'Drugie śniadanie' (second breakfast) is a mid-morning snack, a real Polish institution. 'Na śniadanie' = for breakfast.
The main hot meal, traditionally eaten between 1 and 4 pm. Compare Russian 'обед'. 'Jeść obiad' = to have dinner.
From Latin 'collatio', the light evening meal in monasteries. Usually lighter than 'obiad', eaten around 7 pm.
From 'dać' (to give). 'Pierwsze danie' is the soup, 'drugie danie' the main course, 'danie dnia' the dish of the day.
From French 'dessert'. 'Na deser' = for dessert. Spelled with one 's'.
Related to 'pić' (to drink). Menus list 'napoje' (plural). A cocktail is 'drink' in Polish, borrowed from English.
Related to 'widły' (pitchfork). The '-ec' ending loses its 'e' in other cases: 'widelca'.
Compare Russian 'нож'. Ó becomes o with endings: 'noża', 'noże' (plural).
'Łyżeczka' (diminutive) is a teaspoon. The 'ł' is pronounced like English 'w'.
From German 'Teller'. The final 'rz' is pronounced 'sh' at the end of a word.
From 'szkło' (glass, the material). A wine glass is 'kieliszek', a beer glass 'kufel'.
From Turkish 'fincan', one of several Turkish loans in Polish café vocabulary (like 'kawa'). A mug is 'kubek'.
Built from 'na piwo' (for beer) plus '-ek': a tip is literally 'beer money'. Around 10% is customary in restaurants.
'Wynos' comes from 'wynosić' (to carry out). The opposite is 'na miejscu' (on the spot, to eat in). Staff ask: 'Na miejscu czy na wynos?'
'Pyszne!' is the compliment to give the cook. Older meaning 'proud, haughty', still seen in 'pycha' (pride), which also means 'yum!'.
'Czy' turns any statement into a yes/no question. 'Wolny' means both 'free' and 'slow', so context matters.
A subsidised cafeteria serving cheap home-style Polish food, a survivor of the communist era and still popular. Order at the counter, pay first.
Built on 'droga' (road) with the prefix 'po-': a journey is 'going along the road'. 'Podróżować' = to travel. Feminine despite the consonant ending.
Plural only, from Latin 'vacatio'. Used mainly for the summer break; 'urlop' (from German 'Urlaub') is leave from work.
'Lot' (flight) plus the place suffix '-isko', also seen in 'boisko' (sports field). Warsaw Chopin is 'Lotnisko Chopina'.
From French 'passeport'. The 'sz' spelling shows the word was borrowed by ear: 'pash-port'.
From French 'billet'. Covers bus, train, cinema and museum tickets. 'Bilet ulgowy' is a reduced-price ticket, 'normalny' full price.
Same as English, but the 'h' is pronounced and the stress is on the first syllable: 'HO-tel'. 'W hotelu' = at the hotel.
From Latin 'mappa'. 'Mapa miasta' = city map. A road map is 'mapa drogowa'.
Adverb from 'prosty', which means both 'straight' and 'simple'. 'Proszę iść prosto' = please go straight on.

example.target: Proszę iść prosto, a potem w lewo.

note: 'W' plus accusative for direction; 'na lewo' (on the left) for position. 'Lewy' also means 'dodgy, fake' in slang.
'Prawo' also means 'law' and 'a right' (prawo jazdy = driving licence), the same double meaning as English 'right'.
Adverb; the adjective is 'daleki'. Comparative 'dalej' also means 'next, go on'. 'Czy to daleko?' = Is it far?
'Blisko stąd' = near here. Comparative 'bliżej'. The adjective 'bliski' also means 'close' emotionally.
'Gdzie' corresponds to Russian 'где'. For plural things say 'Gdzie są...?'. The cluster 'gdz' is pronounced as written, 'g-dzh'.

en: How do I get to...? (on foot)
note: 'Dojść' is the perfective of walking somewhere; by vehicle it is 'Jak dojechać do...?'. 'Do' takes the genitive: 'do dworca', 'do rynku'.
Polish past tense shows the speaker's gender: a man says 'zgubiłem się', a woman 'zgubiłam się'. 'Zgubić' = to lose (an object or your way).
From 'krzyż' (cross), which goes back to Latin 'crux'. 'Na skrzyżowaniu' = at the crossroads.
Pan-Slavic word (Russian 'мост'). Warsaw's bridges over the Vistula all carry 'most' in their names.
From 'dwór' (court, manor house); it once meant a courtyard or coaching inn. 'Dworzec Centralny' is Warsaw's main station. A bus station is 'dworzec autobusowy'.
From French 'bagage'. 'Bagaż podręczny' = hand luggage (literally 'hand-held').
From French 'valise' with the diminutive '-ka'. 'Pakować walizkę' = to pack a suitcase.
A Slavic word that German borrowed as 'Grenze'. 'Za granicą' = abroad (literally 'beyond the border', instrumental).
Used for touring places, not visiting people ('odwiedzać'). Perfective 'zwiedzić'. 'Zwiedzanie' = sightseeing.

example.en: We are sightseeing in the old town.

note: Masculine noun ending in '-a', like 'kolega'. Feminine 'turystka'. 'Informacja turystyczna' = tourist information.
'Tu' is the short form, equally common. 'Tutaj' is just 'tu' with an emphatic extension.
Compare Russian 'там'. 'Tam i z powrotem' = there and back (a return ticket is 'bilet w obie strony').
From 'ciągnąć' (to pull), like 'train' from French 'traîner'. The same word also means 'attraction, inclination'. Nasal 'ą' before 'g'.

example.target: Pociąg do Gdańska odjeżdża o dziesiątej.
example.en: The train to Gdańsk leaves at ten.

note: International word; stress on the second-to-last syllable, 'au-TO-bus'. 'Autobusem' (by bus) uses the instrumental.
From English 'tramway'. Trams are the backbone of transport in Kraków, Warsaw, Poznań and Wrocław.
A calque of 'automobile': 'sam' (self) + 'chód' (going, from 'chodzić'). Colloquially 'auto'. 'Samochodem' = by car.
'Taxi' dressed in the Polish suffix '-ówka'. The sign on the roof still says 'TAXI'. 'Taksówkarz' is the driver.
From the British bicycle brand 'Rover', whose safety bicycles were sold in Poland in the 1890s. Pronounced 'RO-ver'.

example.en: I ride to work by bike.

note: 'Sam' (self) + 'lot' (flight), formed like 'samochód'. 'Samolotem' = by plane.
Indeclinable neuter noun. Warsaw is the only Polish city with a metro (two lines).
From 'przystanąć' (to pause). 'Przystanek autobusowy / tramwajowy'. 'Następny przystanek' = next stop, heard on every bus.
From Latin 'statio'. Used for metro and small railway stations and for 'stacja benzynowa' (petrol station); big stations are 'dworzec'.
From French 'perron'. Announcements say 'peron drugi, tor czwarty' (platform two, track four).
From 'kierować' (to steer, drive). Masculine despite '-a'; the rare feminine is 'kierowczyni'. 'Prawo jazdy' = driving licence.
Polish separates going on foot ('iść') from going by vehicle ('jechać'). This is the one-direction form; the habitual form is 'jeździć'.

example.en: I am going to Warsaw by train.

note: Habitual partner 'latać'. Colloquially 'Lecę!' means 'I'm off!' and 'Co leci w kinie?' is 'What's on at the cinema?'
Imperfective; perfective 'wsiąść'. Takes 'do' + genitive: 'wsiadać do autobusu'. Built on 'siadać' (to sit down).
Perfective 'wysiąść'. 'Wysiadam na następnym' = I'm getting off at the next stop. Colloquially also 'to break down' (bateria wysiadła = the battery died).

example.en: Are you getting off? (asked on a crowded bus)

note: From 'przesiadać się' (to change seats, to change trains). 'Bez przesiadki' = direct, no change.
For trains and buses; planes use 'odlot' (away-flight). The board at the station reads 'Odjazdy'.
For wheeled transport; 'przylot' for planes, 'przyjście' for arriving on foot. The root 'jazd-' is 'jazda' (a ride).
'Rozkład' means 'layout, schedule' and 'jazdy' is the genitive of 'jazda' (riding). At the airport it is 'rozkład lotów'.
On Polish buses and trams you must 'skasować bilet' in the yellow machine or face a fine. From 'kasa' (German 'Kasse'). In computing it means 'to delete'.
Literally a cork or stopper (from German 'Kork'): the traffic is bottled up. 'Stać w korku' = to sit in a jam.

example.en: I was late because there was a traffic jam.

note: Also the feminine of the adjective 'drogi' (dear, expensive), so 'droga' can mean 'dear (f.)' in letters. 'W drodze' = on the way.
From German 'Benzin'. A petrol station is 'stacja benzynowa'; diesel is 'olej napędowy' or simply 'diesel'.
An English loan that shifted meaning: 'parking' is the place, not the activity (a false friend). 'Parking podziemny' = underground car park.
A false friend with Russian 'час' (hour). 'Nie mam czasu' = I have no time (genitive after negation). 'Czasami' = sometimes.
Related to Russian 'год' (year), a false friend. 'O której godzinie?' = at what time? 'Pół godziny' = half an hour.
From Latin 'minuta'. 'Pięć minut' uses the genitive plural; 'minutka' (diminutive) = 'just a sec'.
Genitive 'dnia', plural 'dni': the 'ie' vanishes when endings are added. 'Codziennie' = every day.
From Old Slavic 'that same day': the week is the time until the same day comes round. Genitive 'tygodnia', plural 'tygodnie'.

example.en: In a week I go back home.

note: Nasal 'ą'. Originally also 'moon', as in Russian 'месяц', which still has both meanings; Polish now says 'księżyc' for the moon.
The plural is the unrelated 'lata', literally 'summers': 'dwa lata', 'pięć lat'. 'Mam 30 lat' = I am 30.
Short form 'dziś' is just as common. Contains 'dzień' (day) in an old form.
A false friend: Russian 'утро' means 'morning'. 'Do jutra!' = see you tomorrow. 'Pojutrze' = the day after tomorrow.
Compare Russian 'вчера'. 'Przedwczoraj' = the day before yesterday.
'Od teraz' = from now on. The emphatic colloquial 'teraz już' = right now.
Both the noun 'morning' and the adverb 'in the morning'. Compare Russian 'рано' (early): 'wcześnie rano' = early in the morning.
'Południe' means both 'noon' and 'south', just as 'północ' is both 'midnight' and 'north': the compass is named after the sun's position.
Cognate with 'night' and Latin 'nox'. 'W nocy' = at night. Feminine despite the consonant ending.
'Po' (after) + 'niedziela' (Sunday). Polish day names are counted from Monday and are not capitalised. 'W poniedziałek' = on Monday.
From the old word 'wtóry' (second), surviving in 'powtórzyć' (to repeat). Compare Russian 'вторник'.
From 'środek' (middle): the middle of the working week, like German 'Mittwoch'. 'W środę' = on Wednesday.
From 'czwarty' (fourth). 'Tłusty czwartek' (Fat Thursday) is doughnut day before Lent.
From 'piąty' (fifth). Nasal 'ą' before 't'. 'W piątek' = on Friday.

example.en: On Friday we are going to the cinema.

note: From Hebrew 'shabbat' via Greek and Latin, like Italian 'sabato'. 'W sobotę' = on Saturday (accusative).
From 'nie działać' (not to work): the day of rest. 'W niedzielę' = on Sunday.
Polish month names are native Slavic, not Latin: a learner cannot guess them. Not capitalised. 'W styczniu' = in January (locative).
One of only two Latin-based month names in Polish (the other is 'marzec', March). 'W maju' = in May. 'Majówka' is the long weekend of 1-3 May.
From 'gruda' (a frozen lump of earth): the month when the ground freezes hard. 'W grudniu' = in December.
Answered with a feminine ordinal agreeing with 'godzina': 'Jest trzecia' (it's three), 'wpół do czwartej' (half past three, literally 'half to four').

example.en: What time is it? It's five.

note: From Latin 'color'. To ask a colour use the genitive: 'Jakiego koloru jest...?' (of what colour is...?).
The same root is in 'Białystok' and in 'Białoruś' (Belarus, 'White Rus'). Compare Russian 'белый'.
Compare Russian 'чёрный'. 'Czarna kawa' = black coffee. 'Na czarno' means 'off the books'.
From 'czerw', the scale insect (Polish cochineal) once harvested for red dye. The month 'czerwiec' (June) is named after the same insect.
From 'niebo' (sky, heaven), so 'niebieski' also means 'heavenly'. Dark blue is 'granatowy' (from 'granat', pomegranate).
Related to 'zioło' (herb) and 'zieleń' (greenery). Compare Russian 'зелёный'.
Shares its ancient root with 'złoto' (gold) and English 'yellow'. 'Żółty ser' is hard cheese.
From 'pomarańcza' (the fruit), which comes from Italian 'pomo arancio' (orange apple). 'Sok pomarańczowy' = orange juice.
From 'róża' (rose, Latin 'rosa'). 'Widzieć wszystko w różowych kolorach' = to see everything through rose-tinted glasses.
From 'fiolet' (French 'violet'). Polish spells the 'v' sound with 'w' or, in older loans like this, 'f'.
From 'brąz' (bronze, French 'bronze'). Nasal 'ą' pronounced 'on' before 'z'. 'Brązowy medal' = bronze medal.
'Szary człowiek' is an ordinary, anonymous person ('grey man'). 'Szara strefa' = grey economy.
From 'złoto' (gold). The Polish currency is this adjective used as a noun: 'złoty' means 'the golden one'. Plural 'złote', genitive 'złotych'.
From 'srebro' (silver, Russian 'серебро'). The cluster 'srebrn-' is hard; 'srebrny medal' = silver medal.
'Jasnoniebieski' = light blue. The neuter 'Jasne!' means 'Of course! Sure!'. 'Jasne piwo' is lager.
'Ciemnozielony' = dark green. 'Jest ciemno' = it is dark. 'Ciemne piwo' is dark beer.
From German 'Gestalt'. The opening cluster 'kszt' is pronounced exactly as written.
Means circle, wheel and, as a preposition with the genitive, 'near': 'koło dworca' = near the station.
From Latin 'quadratus'. A town square is a different word: 'plac' or 'rynek'. 'Metr kwadratowy' = square metre.
'Trój-' (three) + 'kąt' (angle, corner). 'Kąt' with nasal 'ą' also means the corner of a room.
'Prosty' (straight) + 'kąt' (angle): a shape of right angles. 'Kąt prosty' = right angle.
From Latin 'linea'. Also a bus or tram line: 'linia 4'. Pronounced 'LI-nya'.
Compare Russian 'звезда'. The diminutive 'Gwiazdka' (little star) means Christmas Eve or the Christmas gift-giving.
Diminutive of 'kropla' (drop). It is also the full stop at the end of a sentence and the dot in web addresses.
From 'krąg' (ring, circle). 'Okrągły stół' (Round Table) names the 1989 talks that ended communist rule in Poland.
Compare Russian 'тело'. Also means 'flesh' in a religious sense ('Boże Ciało' = Corpus Christi, a public holiday).
Compare Russian 'голова'. 'Ból głowy' = headache (genitive). 'Mieć głowę do...' = to have a head for something.
The plural 'oczy' is irregular because it preserves an old dual form (things that come in pairs). 'Na oko' = roughly, by eye.
Plural 'uszy', another old dual like 'oczy'. 'Ucho' also means the handle of a cup.
Cognate with English 'nose'. 'Mieć nosa do czegoś' = to have a nose for something.
Plural only and neuter: 'moje usta'. Covers both mouth and lips (a single lip is 'warga').
Plural 'zęby': the nasal 'ą' changes to 'ę', a common alternation. 'Boli mnie ząb' = I have toothache.
One word for hand and arm. Plural 'ręce' (old dual). 'Z ręki' = out of hand; 'ręcznik' (towel) is built on it.
Covers leg and, loosely, foot ('stopa' is the foot itself). 'Na nogach' = on one's feet. Compare Russian 'нога'.
Cognate with Latin 'cor, cordis'; compare Russian 'сердце'. 'Z całego serca' = with all my heart.
The everyday word for stomach area; the organ is 'żołądek'. 'Boli mnie brzuch' = I have a stomach ache.
Plural only: 'bolą mnie plecy' (my back hurts, verb in plural). 'Plecak' (rucksack) is 'the thing on your back'.
Genitive 'krwi': the 'e' disappears. Compare Russian 'кровь'. 'Grupa krwi' = blood group.
From 'lek' (medicine). 'Jestem lekarzem' (I am a doctor) uses the instrumental case, as all professions do after 'być'.

example.en: I need to go to the doctor.

note: From German 'Spital', from Latin 'hospitale', the same source as 'hospital' and 'hotel'. 'W szpitalu' = in hospital.
From Greek 'apothēkē' (storehouse) via German 'Apotheke'. Look for the green cross sign. 'Apteka całodobowa' is open 24 hours.
Plural 'leki'. The longer 'lekarstwo' means the same. 'Lek na kaszel' = cough medicine ('na' + accusative for what it treats).
'Ch' is pronounced 'h'. On its own 'Choroba!' is a mild curse, like 'damn!'. 'Choroba morska' = seasickness.
'Chory na grypę' = ill with flu ('na' + accusative). As a noun, 'chory' is 'the patient'.

example.en: I am ill, I am staying at home.

note: Same root as 'zdrowie' (health) in 'na zdrowie'. Idiom: 'zdrów jak ryba' = fit as a fiddle, literally 'healthy as a fish'.
'Ból głowy' (headache), 'ból gardła' (sore throat), 'ból zęba' (toothache), always with the body part in the genitive.
The body part is the subject and the sufferer is the accusative object ('mnie'): 'the head hurts me'. Plural parts take 'bolą': 'bolą mnie nogi'.
From 'gorący' (hot). 'Mam gorączkę' = I have a fever. Also 'gorączka złota' = gold rush.
From 'zimno' (cold) with the prefix 'prze-' (through). 'Jestem przeziębiony / przeziębiona' = I have a cold.
From Latin 'dens' (tooth). Masculine '-a' noun; feminine 'dentystka'. The formal term is 'stomatolog'.
Cognate with Latin 'domus'. 'W domu' = at home (locative), 'do domu' = homewards (genitive). 'Domek' is a cottage.
The verbal noun of 'mieszkać' (to live, reside). Most city Poles live in a 'mieszkanie' in a 'blok' (apartment block).
The same word means 'peace' ('pokój na świecie' = world peace). Compare Russian 'покой' (rest, calm). Genitive 'pokoju'.
From German 'Küche', ultimately Latin 'coquina'. Like French 'cuisine' it also means a style of cooking: 'kuchnia polska'.
Diminutive of 'łaźnia' (bathhouse). The toilet may be separate and is 'toaleta' or 'WC' (pronounced 'vu-tse').
From 'sypiać' (to sleep habitually) plus the room suffix '-alnia', also in 'jadalnia' (dining room).
Plural only: 'drzwi są otwarte' (the door is open, verb plural). Cognate with English 'door'. The cluster 'drzw' is said as 'd-zhv'.
Derived from 'oko' (eye): a window is the eye of the house. Compare Russian 'окно'. Plural 'okna'.
Ó turns to o when endings are added: 'na stole' (on the table). Compare Russian 'стол'. The restaurant word 'stolik' is its diminutive.
A false friend: Russian 'кресло' means 'armchair'. The Polish armchair is 'fotel' (French 'fauteuil').
Historically a diminutive of 'łoże', which now sounds poetic. 'Iść do łóżka' = to go to bed. Both 'ó' and 'ż' are in the spelling.
International word (Greek 'lampas' via Latin and French). 'Lampka' (diminutive) is a bedside lamp or a small glass of wine.
Compare Russian 'ключ'. Also 'key' in the figurative sense; 'kluczowy' = crucial. Plural 'klucze'.
The inside wall of a room; an outer stone or brick wall is 'mur' (from German 'Mauer'). 'Na ścianie' = on the wall.
Begins with 'pod' (under). For a storey of a building use 'piętro', not 'podłoga'. 'Na podłodze' = on the floor (g changes to dz).
From 'lód' (ice) with the suffix '-ówka'. 'Lody' (plural of ice) means ice cream.
The diminutive of 'kuchnia' names the appliance. 'Kuchenka mikrofalowa' or just 'mikrofalówka' is a microwave.
The set is 'telewizor'; the medium is 'telewizja'. 'Oglądać telewizję' = to watch TV.
Perfective 'posprzątać'. 'Sprzątanie' is housework. Not to be confused with 'myć' (to wash) or 'czyścić' (to clean an object).
From 'gotowy' (ready). Means both 'cook' and 'boil': 'gotować wodę' (boil water). Perfective 'ugotować'.
Only for where you live; 'to be alive' is 'żyć'. Followed by 'w' + locative: 'Mieszkam w Krakowie'.
Floors are counted the British way: 'parter' is the ground floor and 'pierwsze piętro' is the first floor above it. Nasal 'ę'.
From German 'Winde' (winch). 'Jechać windą' = to take the lift (instrumental).
From Italian 'balcone' via French. 'Na balkonie' = on the balcony. Standard in Polish apartment blocks.
From 'grodzić' (to fence in), the root also behind 'gród' (stronghold) and Russian 'город' (city). 'Ogródek' is a small garden or allotment.
From 'ubierać' (to dress). Often plural: 'ubrania'. 'Ubrany' = dressed.
From Latin 'casula' (a hooded cloak), the same source as 'chasuble'. 'Koszula nocna' = nightdress.
The diminutive of 'koszula' means a T-shirt or sports jersey. 'T-shirt' is also used.
Plural only, like 'trousers'. From 'spód' (underside): they were once the garment worn underneath. 'Spodenki' = shorts.
Diminutive of 'suknia' (gown), which is now mostly 'suknia ślubna' (wedding dress). 'W sukience' = in a dress.
Also built on 'spód' (bottom, underside). 'Spódniczka' is a short skirt.
A casual or outdoor jacket; a suit jacket is 'marynarka' (literally 'sailor's thing'). 'Kurtka zimowa' = winter jacket.

example.en: Take a jacket, it is cold.

note: Compare Russian 'плащ'. 'Płaszcz przeciwdeszczowy' = raincoat (literally 'against-rain').
From English 'sweater', respelled by ear; the 'w' is a 'v' sound. Plural 'swetry'.
Plural of 'but'; covers shoes and boots. Related to French 'botte'. Poles take their shoes off indoors: 'zdjąć buty'.
Diminutive of 'skarpeta', from Italian 'scarpetta' (little shoe). Singular 'skarpetka'.
Any brimless hat, including a woolly winter hat. Related to English 'cap' through Latin 'cappa'. A brimmed hat is 'kapelusz'.
Diminutive of 'szal' (shawl), a word that travelled from Persian through French 'châle'. Fans wear a 'szalik' in club colours.
From 'rękaw' (sleeve), itself from 'ręka' (hand). Singular 'rękawiczka'.
Diminutive of 'pas' (belt, zone). Also means a stripe: 'w paski' = striped.
A Turkic loanword (Turkish 'torba'). 'Torebka' (diminutive) = handbag; 'torba na zakupy' = shopping bag.
Plural only, from Latin 'ocularis'. 'Okulary przeciwsłoneczne' = sunglasses (literally 'against-sun').
Diminutive of 'zegar' (clock), from Middle High German 'seiger'. 'Zegar' is on the wall, 'zegarek' on the wrist.
Both 'wear' and 'carry (habitually)'. The one-trip form is 'nieść'. 'Nosić okulary / brodę' = to wear glasses / a beard.
'Ubierać' alone means to dress someone else; 'się' makes it reflexive. A false friend: Russian 'убирать' means 'to tidy up'. Perfective 'ubrać się'.
'Jaki rozmiar?' = what size? Poland uses European sizes (38, 40...) for clothes and shoes.

example.target: Czy jest to w większym rozmiarze?
example.en: Do you have this in a bigger size?

note: From 'biały' (white): linen was traditionally white. Also means bed linen ('bielizna pościelowa').
English 'jeans' in Polish spelling: 'dż' is the 'j' of 'jeans'. Plural only, like 'spodnie'.
From French 'garniture' (a matching set). The jacket of a suit is 'marynarka'. A woman's suit is 'kostium' or 'garsonka'.
From Italian 'cappello'. The 'sz' ending is pronounced 'sh'. 'Kapelusz słomkowy' = straw hat.
Compare Czech 'práce'. 'W pracy' = at work, 'do pracy' = to work. 'Praca domowa' = homework.
The '-ować' verbs conjugate with '-uję'. 'Pracować jako kelner' = to work as a waiter. Imperfective only.
From French 'bureau'. 'W biurze' = at the office. 'Biuro podróży' = travel agency.
From Italian 'firma' (signature) via German. 'Pracuję w firmie...' = I work at a company called...
From French 'chef', spelled with Polish 'sz'. Feminine 'szefowa'. Waiters sometimes call a male customer 'szefie' (vocative).
From 'praca'. Masculine personal nouns in '-nik' form the feminine with '-nica': 'pracownica'. Plural 'pracownicy'.
Only for university students; school pupils are 'uczniowie'. 'Jestem studentem / studentką' uses the instrumental.

example.en: I am a student (f.) in Warsaw.

note: From 'uczyć' (to teach). The 'e' drops in other forms: 'ucznia', plural 'uczniowie'. Feminine 'uczennica'.
From Latin 'schola'. 'Szkoła podstawowa' = primary school, 'liceum' = secondary school. 'W szkole' = at school.
'Uniwersytet Jagielloński' in Kraków (1364) is Poland's oldest. 'Na uniwersytecie' = at university ('na', not 'w').
From Latin 'lectio' (a reading). 'Lekcja polskiego' = Polish lesson (genitive of the language).
From Latin 'examen'. 'Zdawać egzamin' is to take an exam, 'zdać egzamin' (perfective) is to pass it: aspect makes the difference.
Formally the diminutive of 'księga' (a big tome, a register), but it is the ordinary word. 'Księgarnia' = bookshop.

example.en: I am reading an interesting book.

note: From 'zszyć' (to sew together): pages stitched into a booklet. A laptop-type notebook is 'notebook' or 'laptop'.
'Długo' (long) + 'pis-' (write): a pen that writes for a long time. A fountain pen is 'pióro' (feather).
From English, with 'k' for 'c'. 'Na komputerze' = on the computer. A laptop is 'laptop'.
'Uczyć' is 'to teach'; adding 'się' turns it into 'to learn'. The subject learned goes in the genitive: 'uczę się polskiego'.

example.en: I have been learning Polish for a year.

note: Compare Russian 'читать'. Perfective 'przeczytać' (to read through). 'Czytelnik' = reader.
The 's' softens to 'sz' in the present tense: 'piszę'. Perfective 'napisać'. 'Pisarz' = writer.
Means both the tongue in your mouth and a language, like French 'langue'. 'Język polski' = the Polish language. Nasal 'ę'.
Compare Russian 'слово'. One theory derives 'Słowianie' (the Slavs) from it: 'people who share the word'. 'Słownik' = dictionary.
From 'pytać' (to ask a question), not 'prosić' (to ask for something). 'Mam pytanie' = I have a question.
Feminine despite the consonant ending. From 'odpowiadać' (to answer); 'odpowiedzialność' (responsibility) is from the same root, as in English.
From 'spotkać się' (to meet). Used for business meetings and for dates alike. 'Na spotkaniu' = at the meeting.
Curiously the same word means 'disappointment'. 'Z zawodu jestem...' = by profession I am... 'Zawodowy' = professional.
Originally 'good weather', and still so in 'jest pogoda' (it's fine); bad weather is 'niepogoda'. 'Jaka jest pogoda?' = what's the weather like?
Compare Russian 'солнце', where the 'l' is silent; in Polish the 'ł' is pronounced as 'w'. 'Świeci słońce' = the sun is shining.
Compare Russian 'дождь'. The ending 'szcz' is one of the famous Polish clusters, pronounced 'shch'.
Cognate with English 'snow'. 'Pada śnieg' = it is snowing. 'Bałwan' is a snowman (and also an idiot).
Cognate with 'wind' and Latin 'ventus'. 'Wieje wiatr' = the wind is blowing. 'Halny' is the warm mountain wind of the Tatras.
A rain cloud; a fluffy fair-weather cloud is 'obłok'. 'Jest pochmurno' = it is cloudy.
Compare Russian 'буря'. A thunderstorm is 'burza z piorunami' (with lightning bolts).
Compare Russian 'мгла' (haze). The initial 'mg' cluster has no vowel; just run the two consonants together.
From Latin. Poland uses Celsius; 'minus pięć stopni' = minus five degrees.
'Jest ciepło' = it is warm; 'jest mi ciepło' = I am warm (dative). The adjective is 'ciepły'. Compare Russian 'тепло'.
'Jest mi zimno' = I am cold, literally 'it is cold to me'; never 'jestem zimny', which would mean a cold personality. Adjective 'zimny'.
'Jest gorąco' = it is hot; adjective 'gorący' (hot to the touch, also 'passionate'). Nasal 'ą' pronounced 'on'.
'Padać' means 'to fall'; 'pada śnieg' = it is snowing. Poles often just say 'Pada' for 'it's raining'.
Also the plural of 'rok' (year): 'dwa lata' = two years, counting in summers. 'Latem' = in summer (instrumental).
Cognate with Latin 'hiems'. 'Zimą' = in winter. The root gives 'zimno' (cold) and 'zimny'.
Compare Russian 'весна'. 'Wiosną' = in spring. The spelling 'wio' shows a vowel shift that Russian lacks.
Compare Russian 'осень'. Feminine. 'Jesienią' = in autumn. 'Złota polska jesień' (golden Polish autumn) is a stock phrase.
Means both a tree and wood as a material. Cognate with English 'tree' via Indo-European. Compare Russian 'дерево'.
Related to Russian 'цвет' (colour) and 'цветок' (flower). Diminutive 'kwiatek'; plural 'kwiaty'. 'Kwiaciarnia' = florist's.
Compare Russian 'лес'. 'W lesie' = in the forest (note the a/e change). Mushroom picking in the 'las' is a national pastime.
Compare Russian 'река'; Polish 'rz' corresponds to a soft Russian 'r'. The Wisła (Vistula) is Poland's longest river.
Cognate with Latin 'mare'. 'Nad morzem' = at the seaside, literally 'above the sea' (instrumental). Sounds identical to 'może' (maybe).

example.en: In summer we go to the seaside.

note: Also means 'top' and 'upstairs': 'na górze' = upstairs. Compare Russian 'гора'. The Tatry are Poland's highest mountains ('w górach' = in the mountains).
Compare Russian 'озеро'. Masuria in the north-east is 'kraina tysiąca jezior' (land of a thousand lakes). 'Nad jeziorem' = by the lake.
Sky and heaven are one word; 'niebieski' (blue) is 'sky-coloured'. Plural 'niebiosa' is used for heaven in religious language.
A false friend: Russian 'склеп' means 'crypt'. Both go back to a word for a vault; Polish shops were once vaulted cellars. 'W sklepie' = in the shop.
Plural only, with nasal 'ą'. From Old High German 'pfenning', the same word as English 'penny'. 'Nie mam pieniędzy' = I have no money (genitive).
From Latin 'grossus' (thick coin) via Czech 'groš', related to German 'Groschen'. 'Nie mam ani grosza' = I haven't a penny.
Compare Russian 'цена'. 'Cennik' = price list. 'W dobrej cenie' = at a good price.
'Ile' asks for a quantity. The shorter 'Ile płacę?' (how much do I pay?) is used when settling up.
Like English 'dear', it means both costly and beloved: letters begin 'Drogi Piotrze' / 'Droga Anno'. Comparative 'droższy'.
Soft stem: masculine 'tani', feminine 'tania'. 'Taniej' = cheaper, 'tanio' = cheaply.
Imperfective; the perfective 'kupić' is used for a single completed purchase ('kupiłem chleb'). An early Germanic loan into Slavic, related to 'cheap'.

example.en: I buy bread at the bakery.

note: Perfective 'zapłacić'. The means of payment takes the instrumental: 'płacić kartą / gotówką' (by card / in cash).
From German 'kosten'. Mostly in the third person: 'to kosztuje', 'one kosztują'. Also 'to taste, to sample' in older usage.
Shop staff ask 'Kartą czy gotówką?' (card or cash?). Contactless payment is near-universal in Poland.
From 'gotowy' (ready), like English 'ready money'. 'Gotówką' = in cash (instrumental).
Means both 'the rest' and the change you get back: 'Reszty nie trzeba' = keep the change (genitive after negation).
The till receipt; an invoice is 'faktura'. Cashiers ask 'Paragon?' before printing it.
From Italian 'cassa' via German 'Kasse'. 'Proszę do kasy' = please go to the checkout. In slang 'kasa' simply means money.
Also 'bargaining': 'targować się' = to haggle. 'Targi' (plural) are trade fairs, as in the Poznań fairs.
From 'piec' (to bake) plus '-arnia'. 'Piekarz' is the baker. Polish bakeries also sell 'bułki' (bread rolls).
'Spożywczy' comes from 'spożywać' (to consume). Often shortened to 'spożywczak' in speech.
'Handel' (trade) is a German loan. Big malls are also called 'galeria'. 'Centrum' is neuter and does not decline in the singular.
A partial false friend: 'promocja' in a shop means a discount or deal, not promotion at work ('awans'). 'W promocji' = on offer.
'Bank' + 'automat'. 'Wypłacić pieniądze z bankomatu' = withdraw money from an ATM.
From Italian 'banco'. 'Konto w banku' = a bank account; 'przelew' = a bank transfer.
From German 'Kontor' (office). Polish 'kantory' usually give better rates than banks or airport desks. 'Kurs' = exchange rate.
Shop signs use the neuter 'Otwarte' / 'Zamknięte' (open / closed). 'Otwarty' also means open-minded.

example.en: The shop is open until 8 pm.

note: Diminutive of 'kosz' (basket). Also the online shopping cart button. A supermarket trolley is 'wózek'.
From 'szczęście' (happiness, luck). The opening 'szcz' is said 'shch'. 'Szczęśliwej podróży!' = have a good trip.
From 'smutek' (sadness). 'Smutno mi' = I feel sad (adverb + dative), the usual way to express a mood.
Past participle of 'zmęczyć' (to tire out), from 'męka' (torment). Nasal 'ę'. 'Jestem zmęczony / zmęczona'.
Contains 'wola' (will): to be satisfied is to have things to your will. 'Zadowolony z' + genitive: 'zadowolony z pracy'.
From 'nerw' (nerve), but broader than English 'nervous': it covers irritated, upset and stressed. 'Nie denerwuj się' = don't get worked up.
From 'nuda' (boredom). 'Nudzę się' = I'm bored; 'nudny' = boring. Do not confuse the two as English learners often do.
From 'głód' (hunger); compare Russian 'голодный'. 'Jestem głodny jak wilk' = I'm as hungry as a wolf.

example.en: I'm hungry. Shall we go and eat something?

note: 'Wesołych Świąt!' = Merry Christmas (genitive plural, because wishes take the genitive). Compare Russian 'весёлый'.
From 'sam' (alone, oneself). Means both lonely and unattached; 'samotna matka' = single mother.
From 'pokój' (peace). 'Spokojnie!' = take it easy. 'Spokojnej nocy' = have a peaceful night.
Takes the accusative: 'kocham cię'. 'Kochanie' = darling, 'kochany' = beloved (often used as 'dear' in letters).
A false friend: Russian 'любить' means 'to love', but Polish 'lubić' is only 'to like'. 'Lubię cię' = I like you; 'Lubię kawę'.
'Cieszę się!' = I'm glad. What you are glad about takes 'z' + genitive: 'cieszę się z prezentu'. 'Cieszę się na' = I'm looking forward to.
Built on 'martwy' (dead): worry literally deadens you. 'Martwić się o' + accusative: 'martwię się o ciebie' (I worry about you).
Always reflexive and followed by the genitive: 'boję się psów' (I'm afraid of dogs). The stem changes: 'bać' but 'boję'.
Irregular: 'chcę' with nasal 'ę'. The polite form is the conditional 'chciałbym / chciałabym' (I would like, m./f.). Compare Russian 'хотеть'.
'Jak się czujesz?' = how do you feel? Answer with an adverb: 'czuję się dobrze / źle'. Without 'się', 'czuć' means to smell or sense something.
Followed by 'za' + instrumental: 'tęsknię za tobą' (I miss you), 'tęsknię za Polską'. Nasal 'ę'. 'Tęsknota' = longing.
From 'miły', which once meant 'beloved' and now means 'nice, kind'. Feminine, like all nouns in '-ość'. 'Miłość od pierwszego wejrzenia' = love at first sight.
From 'rad' (glad), as in 'rad jestem' (I'm glad). 'Z radością' = gladly, with pleasure (instrumental).
Compare Russian 'страх'. 'Strach się bać!' is a colloquial 'scary stuff!'. 'Straszny' = terrible, 'strasznie' = terribly (also 'very').
One word for both happiness and luck: 'mam szczęście' = I'm lucky, 'na szczęście' = fortunately. 'Nieszczęście' = misfortune.
'Cię' is the short, unstressed accusative of 'ty'; the stressed form 'ciebie' goes first for emphasis: 'Ciebie kocham'.
The imperative of 'martwić się'. To more than one person, or politely: 'Niech się pan nie martwi'. 'Spoko' is the slang equivalent.

en: I feel like sleeping / I'm sleepy
note: An impersonal pattern with the dative: 'chce mi się pić' = I'm thirsty, 'nie chce mi się' = I can't be bothered.
The one-direction form; the habitual form is 'chodzić'. Irregular past 'szedł / szła'. 'Idę do domu' = I'm going home.

example.en: Shall we go for a coffee?

note: The habitual partner of 'iść': 'chodzę do szkoły' (I go to school). Compare Russian 'ходить'. 'Chodzić z kimś' = to date someone.
Cognate with 'eat' and Latin 'edere'. Irregular present ('jem', 'jedzą'); perfective 'zjeść'. 'Jem śniadanie' = I'm having breakfast.

example.en: What do you eat for breakfast?

note: Compare Russian 'пить'. 'Piwo' (beer) and 'napój' (drink) come from this root. Perfective 'wypić'.
The present tense softens the 's' to 'ś': 'śpię'. Compare Russian 'спать'. 'Dobrze spałem' = I slept well.
Imperfective; perfective 'wstać'. 'Wstaję o siódmej' = I get up at seven (ordinal in the locative).

example.en: What time do you get up?

note: Without 'się' it takes an object: 'myć zęby' (brush teeth), 'myć naczynia' (wash the dishes). Perfective 'umyć'.
Perfective 'zrobić'. Related to 'robota' (work), the Czech word that gave English 'robot'. 'Co robisz?' = What are you doing?

example.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

note: 'Mówię po polsku' = I speak Polish ('po' + a special '-u' form of the adjective). Perfective 'powiedzieć'. 'Mowa' = speech.

example.en: Do you speak English? (to a man)

note: Built on 'rozum' (reason, mind). 'Nie rozumiem' is the learner's most useful sentence. Perfective 'zrozumieć'.
For facts and information ('wiem, że...'); knowing people or places is 'znać'. Same Indo-European root as English 'wit' and 'wise'. 'Nie wiem' = I don't know.
For people, places and languages: 'znam Kraków', 'znam go'. Compare Russian 'знать' and the Greek root of 'gnosis'. 'Znajomy' = acquaintance.
Irregular present 'mam'. Used for age ('mam 30 lat') and names ('mam na imię'). Negated, the object goes into the genitive: 'nie mam czasu'.
'Czy mogę?' = May I? The third person 'może' doubles as the word 'maybe'. The 'g' softens to 'ż' in most forms. Compare Russian 'мочь'.
A loan from German 'müssen'. 'Muszę iść' = I have to go. 'Nie musisz' = you don't have to (not 'you mustn't', which is 'nie wolno').
'Do widzenia' (goodbye) is 'until seeing' from this verb. Perfective 'zobaczyć'. 'Widzę' = I see, also 'I get it'.
Takes the genitive: 'słucham muzyki' (I listen to music), 'słuchaj mnie'. 'Słucham?' is also 'Pardon?' and 'Hello?' on the phone.
For TV, films and exhibitions: 'oglądać telewizję'. Perfective 'obejrzeć'. Nasal 'ą' in every form.

example.en: In the evening we watch a film.

note: Imperfective; perfective 'dać'. The recipient takes the dative: 'daję to mamie'. Cognate with Latin 'dare'. 'Daj mi' = give me.
Present stem 'bior-/bierz-'. The perfective is the unrelated 'wziąć' ('wezmę' = I'll take). Compare Russian 'брать'.
From 'dzwon' (bell). 'Dzwonić do' + genitive: 'dzwonię do mamy'. Perfective 'zadzwonić'. 'Zadzwoń do mnie' = call me.
Imperfective; perfective 'otworzyć'. 'Otwarty' (open) is its participle. 'Otwieramy o dziewiątej' = we open at nine.
Perfective 'zamknąć'. 'Zamknięte' = closed (on signs). The same root gives 'zamek' (lock, castle).
From 'moc' (power): to help is to lend strength. Takes the dative: 'pomagam mamie'. Perfective 'pomóc'. 'Pomocy!' = Help!
'Czekać na' + accusative: 'czekam na autobus'. Perfective 'poczekać'; 'Poczekaj!' = wait a moment. 'Poczekalnia' = waiting room.

example.en: I'm waiting for you in front of the cinema.

note: Compare Russian 'что'. 'Co to jest?' = What is this? Declines: 'czego' (genitive), 'czym' (instrumental).
'Kto to?' = Who is that? Declines like a noun: 'kogo' (whom), 'komu' (to whom), 'z kim' (with whom).
Polish separates 'gdzie' (where, location) from 'dokąd' (where to, direction): 'Dokąd idziesz?' = Where are you going?
Also the conjunction 'when' in statements: 'kiedy byłem mały' (when I was little). 'Kiedyś' = once, some day.
'Dla' (for) + 'czego' (genitive of 'co'). The answer starts with 'bo' or 'dlatego, że' (because).
Also 'as, like': 'zimny jak lód' (cold as ice). 'Jak się masz?' = how are you. 'Jakoś' = somehow.
One word for both, followed by the genitive: 'ile czasu?' (how much time), 'ile osób?' (how many people). 'Ile masz lat?' = How old are you?
Agrees like an adjective (który, która, które). Also the relative 'who/which': 'człowiek, który...'. 'O której?' = at what time?
Asks for a description, not a choice: 'Jaki jest twój dom?' (what is your house like?). Agrees: jaki, jaka, jakie. 'Jaki piękny!' = how beautiful!
Starts a yes/no question and has no English equivalent: 'Czy masz czas?' = Do you have time? In speech it is often dropped and the voice rises instead. Also 'whether'.
Pronounced 'ee'. Compare Russian 'и'. For contrast ('and yet, while') Polish uses 'a' instead: 'ja piję kawę, a ty herbatę'.
Also an exclamation of surprise: 'Ale pięknie!' (how beautiful!), 'Ale zimno!' (it's so cold!).
'Albo... albo' = either... or. 'Lub' is a more formal synonym. In questions use 'czy': 'kawa czy herbata?'

example.en: Coffee or tea, it's all the same.

note: The everyday word; 'ponieważ' and 'dlatego, że' are more formal. Always preceded by a comma: 'Nie idę, bo pada'.
Introduces reported speech and thoughts: 'Myślę, że...' (I think that...). Polish always puts a comma before 'że'. Not the demonstrative 'that' ('to', 'tamten').

example.en: I know that you are right.

note: 'Bardzo dziękuję' = thank you very much. Also 'very much' with verbs: 'bardzo lubię'. Comparative 'bardziej' = more.
'Ja też' = me too. In negatives it means 'either': 'ja też nie' (me neither). A near-synonym is 'także'.
'Nie tylko..., ale też...' = not only... but also. 'Tylko nie to!' = anything but that!
'Już nie' = no longer, 'już idę' = I'm coming (right now). Compare Russian 'уже'.
'Jeszcze nie' = not yet, 'jeszcze raz' = once more, 'jeszcze jedno piwo' = another beer. The 'szcz' cluster is pronounced 'shch'.
Literally the third person of 'móc' (can): 'it may be'. 'Być może' = perhaps. Sounds identical to 'morze' (sea).
'Na zawsze' = forever. 'Jak zawsze' = as always. Compare Russian 'всегда', a different formation.
Must be paired with 'nie' (double negative): 'nigdy nie byłem w Polsce' = I have never been to Poland.
Needs 'nie' with the verb: 'nic nie wiem' (I know nothing). 'Nic takiego' = nothing special. Genitive 'niczego'.
'Wszystko w porządku' = everything's fine. 'Wszystko jedno' = it makes no difference. The people form is 'wszyscy' (everybody).
Compare Russian 'добрый', which has narrowed to 'kind'. Adverb 'dobrze' (well). Comparative 'lepszy' is from a different root, like English 'better'.
Means both 'bad' and 'angry': 'jestem zły' = I'm angry. Adverb 'źle' (badly). Comparative 'gorszy' is from another root, like 'worse'.
The everyday word; 'wielki' means great or huge. 'Duże piwo' = a large beer. Comparative 'większy'.
Compare Russian 'малый'. Polish loves diminutives: 'malutki', 'maleńki' (tiny). Comparative 'mniejszy'.
Cognate with 'new' and Latin 'novus'. 'Nowy Rok' = New Year. 'Co nowego?' = what's new? (genitive).
Compare Russian 'старый'. 'Stare Miasto' = Old Town. Colloquially 'stary' is also 'mate, dude' and 'starzy' = parents.
Compare Russian 'молодой' with its extra vowel. 'Młoda para' = the newly-weds. 'Młodzież' = young people.
Milder than 'piękny'. Used of weather too: 'ładna pogoda'. Adverb 'ładnie' = nicely.
Nasal 'ę'. 'Piękno' = beauty. 'Pięknie dziękuję' = thank you so much (literally 'beautifully').
Also of weather: 'brzydka pogoda' = nasty weather. 'Brzydkie słowo' = a swear word. The 'rz' is said 'zh'.
One word for both, like German 'hoch'. Compare Russian 'высокий'. Comparative 'wyższy', adverb 'wysoko'.
Of people, prices and temperatures: 'niska cena' = low price. Compare Russian 'низкий'. Comparative 'niższy'.
Same root as 'dług' (debt): something owed over a long time. Adverb 'długo' = for a long time. Comparative 'dłuższy'.
For things and time, not people's height (that is 'niski'). Compare Russian 'короткий'. 'Krótko mówiąc' = in short.
Adverb 'szybko' (quickly), heard constantly: 'Szybko!' = hurry up! Comparative 'szybszy'.
Two meanings: slow ('wolny pociąg') and free ('wolny stolik', 'wolny czas'). Adverb 'wolno' = slowly, and also 'it is allowed'.
Adverb 'łatwo' (easily). 'To nie jest łatwe' = it isn't easy (neuter agreeing with 'to').
From 'trud' (toil, effort); compare Russian 'труд' (labour). 'Polski jest trudny' is what every learner says. Adverb 'trudno' also means 'tough luck, never mind'.
From 'waga' (weight, German 'Waage'): important = weighty. Also 'valid': 'bilet jest ważny' = the ticket is valid.
Of things 'interesting', of people 'curious': 'jestem ciekawy, czy...' = I wonder whether... 'Ciekawostka' = a fun fact.
Compare Russian 'чистый'. 'Czysta' on a bottle means plain unflavoured vodka. 'Czyste powietrze' = clean air.
From 'brud' (dirt). 'Brudne naczynia' = dirty dishes. 'Brudno' = it's dirty (adverb).
From 'moc' (power). For coffee, tea, alcohol and medicine: 'mocna kawa'. Physical strength of people is 'silny'.
Compare Russian 'слабый'. 'Słabo mi' = I feel faint. Colloquially 'słabe' means 'lame, poor' (of a film, a joke).
From 'ciężar' (weight, burden). Means heavy and also hard or tough: 'ciężka praca' = hard work, 'ciężki dzień' = a rough day.
A false friend: Russian 'место' means 'place' (Russian for city is 'город'). 'W mieście' = in town (note the s/ś change).

example.en: I live in a small town.

note: Feminine. 'Na wsi' = in the country, 'na wieś' = to the country ('na', not 'w'). 'Wiejski' = rural, as in 'chleb wiejski'.
Compare Russian 'улица'. Addresses abbreviate it 'ul.': 'ul. Długa 5'. 'Na ulicy' = in the street.
From German 'Ring': medieval markets were held in a ring of houses. Kraków's 'Rynek Główny' is one of the largest medieval squares in Europe. Also 'the market' in economics.
From German 'Rathaus' (Rat = council, Haus = house). Many Polish town halls stand in the middle of the 'rynek'.
From Latin 'castellum' (fort) via Old Czech 'kostel'. Ó becomes o in other cases: 'do kościoła'. Note the 'ść' and 'ł' spelling.
From German 'Platz'. 'Plac Zamkowy' = Castle Square in Warsaw. Also a building site ('plac budowy').
Same as English. 'W parku' = in the park. Warsaw's 'Łazienki' park hosts free Chopin concerts in summer.
Latin neuter: it does not change in the singular ('w muzeum') but the plural is 'muzea'. Many museums are free one day a week.
From Greek via Latin and French. 'Do teatru' = to the theatre. Pronounced 'TE-atr', two syllables.
From German 'Kino', short for 'Kinematograph'. 'Do kina' = to the cinema, 'w kinie' = at the cinema. Films are usually subtitled, not dubbed.

example.en: Shall we go to the cinema today?

note: From Greek 'bibliothēkē'. A library, not a bookshop (which is 'księgarnia'). 'W bibliotece' = in the library.
From Italian 'posta' via German. 'Poczta Polska' is the national post. 'Na poczcie' = at the post office (note the t/c change).
One word for a castle, a door lock and a zip fastener, all from 'zamykać' (to close). 'Zamek Królewski' = the Royal Castle in Warsaw.
Latin neuter, unchanging in the singular: 'w centrum' = in the centre, 'do centrum' = to the centre. 'Centrum miasta' = city centre.
From 'dzielić' (to divide): a division of the city. Warsaw has 18 of them. 'W jakiej dzielnicy mieszkasz?' = which district do you live in?
From 'budować' (to build). The 'e' drops in other forms: 'budynku'. 'Budowa' = a construction site.
From 'kamień' (stone): a masonry house as opposed to a wooden one. The typical old-town apartment building with a courtyard.
From French 'toilette'. Doors are marked 'damska' (ladies) and 'męska' (gents), or with a circle (women) and a triangle (men).

example.en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

note: From Latin 'politia'. The emergency number is 112 (or 997 for police alone). A police officer is 'policjant / policjantka'.
Nasal 'ą'; genitive 'urzędu'. 'Urząd miasta' = city hall offices, 'urząd pocztowy' = post office. A clerk is 'urzędnik'.
Capitalised as a name: 'Stare Miasto'. Warsaw's was rebuilt from rubble after 1944 and is a UNESCO site. 'Na Starym Mieście' = in the Old Town.
Related to 'pamięć' (memory): a monument is a thing for remembering. 'Pomnik Mickiewicza' stands on Kraków's main square.
From 'osiedlić się' (to settle). The typical Polish residential neighbourhood of apartment blocks ('bloki'). 'Na osiedlu' = on the estate.
From French 'adresse', with one 'd'. 'Jaki jest twój adres?' = what is your address? Postcodes look like '00-001'.
